prompt.context: Your client is a global mining company with a location in South Africa. This particular location is performing below average financially. McKinsey has been hired to identify the problem and make recommendations to address it.
prompt.question: What would you do first to approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: Where is the processing plant located and how does it move product to customers?
clarifying_info.a: The processing plant is located 160 miles inland and uses a fleet of large trucks to transport minerals from the plant (located near the mineral source) to a port city. The minerals are then loaded onto barges and shipped to clients around the world.

clarifying_info.q: What does the plant need to do operationally?
clarifying_info.a: The plant needs to operate at maximum capacity to meet customer demand.

clarifying_info.q: What type of minerals/products does it produce?
clarifying_info.a: The minerals produced are commodities with low margins.

exhibits.title: Mighty Mining Trip Time Distribution
exhibits.shows: A histogram showing the distribution of total round-trip times (in hours) for truck trips from the plant to the port and back. The x-axis shows total round trip time in hours (up to 24) and the y-axis shows number of trips (up to 1000).

data.notable_feature: Bimodal distribution with two distinct peaks

framework: Revenues: explore historical data, trends, product-specific data; benchmark against competitors and other corporate locations

Operations: explore operational issues that might lead to poor performance — interruptions (is plant at full capacity, power outages, local protests, theft/unrest), employee skill level, employee morale
Costs: explore fixed costs (PP&E, overhead) and variable costs (materials, labor)
Transportation: since product is a commodity, transportation makes up a large portion of product cost and should be separated out — COGS breakdown includes Labor, Materials, Shipping/Logistics

questions.prompt: Transportation costs are significantly higher as a portion of COGS than any other African plant location. Why might this be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate a range of creative, out-of-the-box ideas. Strong answers include: trucks leaving less than full (increasing number of trips needed); poor route planning or drivers not going directly to the port; drivers sleeping on the job or taking excessive breaks; trucks being hijacked along the route; drivers paying bribes to get through roadblocks.

questions.prompt: You collect historical data on the average time it takes a truck to make the 200-mile trip from the plant to the port. What should you expect the graph to look like, and what can you draw from the actual data shown in Exhibit 1?
questions.guidance: Expected distribution is a normal (bell-curve) distribution around the typical trip time. The actual data shows a bimodal (two-peaked) distribution. The first peak is expected. The second peak requires explanation — possible causes include certain drivers taking too many breaks, traffic patterns at certain times of day, or drivers making unauthorized stops. Candidate should flag the second peak as an anomaly requiring further investigation.

questions.prompt: You discover that the port closes at 10pm and any truck that does not arrive by 10pm must wait until the port opens again at 4am to drop off its load and return to the plant. The minimum round-trip travel time is 7 hours and the plant owns 20 trucks. A barge needs 30 truckloads to reach capacity and ship out. What would you recommend Mighty Mining do about this situation? (Remember: the plant must operate at max capacity to meet customer demand.)
questions.guidance: Rather than optimizing with exact numbers, the candidate should identify multiple bottlenecks: (1) travel time constraints against the 10pm port closing, (2) port hours of operation limiting delivery windows, (3) mismatch between truck fleet capacity (20 trucks) and barge loading requirement (30 truckloads). Strong answers propose both short-term and long-term solutions — see recommendation section.

math.setup: Minimum round-trip = 7 hours. Port closes at 10pm, opens at 4am. Fleet = 20 trucks. Barge capacity = 30 truckloads. Identify latest departure time that still hits the 10pm cut-off: latest departure = 10pm minus 7 hours = 3pm. Trucks departing after 3pm risk missing the port cut-off. With 20 trucks and a 7-hour minimum cycle, consider how many loads per day can realistically be delivered before 10pm.
steps: If a truck leaves at or before 3pm it can make the 10pm cut-off; trucks leaving after 3pm must wait at port from arrival until 4am
To fill one barge (30 loads) with 20 trucks: at minimum 2 full cycles needed (20 + 10), but port timing constrains how many cycles fit in a day
Focus on maximizing trucks that depart before 3pm and return in time for another run before cut-off
math.answer: The key insight is not a single optimized number but the identification of three bottlenecks (travel time, port hours, fleet vs. barge size) and that missing the 10pm cut-off adds a 6-hour wait penalty (10pm to 4am), severely cutting daily throughput.

brainstorming.prompt: What might explain the second peak in the bimodal trip-time distribution?

categories.name: Driver behavior
ideas: Certain drivers taking excessive breaks or sleeping en route
Unauthorized personal stops along the 160-mile route

categories.name: Traffic and road conditions
ideas: Rush-hour traffic patterns at certain times of day
Road construction or seasonal road closures
Roadblocks requiring bribe payments causing delays

categories.name: Security/external issues
ideas: Truck hijackings causing long delays while awaiting resolution
Escorts or convoys required at certain times adding travel time

categories.name: Operational/loading
ideas: Delays at the port queue during peak arrival windows
Trucks waiting for a full load before departing the plant

recommendation: Short term: identify the latest a truck can leave and still arrive by 10pm (3pm departure for a 7-hour minimum trip); use driver incentive programs to reduce rest stops and meet the cut-off; rearrange driver shifts to optimize material delivered to the port before 10pm
Long term: lobby for 24-hour port operations, which would be more profitable for all parties
Evaluate cost of setting up a storage facility near the port for night deliveries versus purchasing more trucks
Analyze the cost of upgrading the fleet to larger trucks to reduce the number of trips needed to fill a barge (currently 30 loads with 20 trucks)
Consider leasing trucks versus purchasing to reduce capital requirements
risks: Since the location is already underperforming, must analyze cost of capital to ensure any capital improvement is the highest-NPV alternative (e.g., could it be more profitable to ship from a better-performing plant?)
Changes in customer demand could render a capital investment unnecessary in the long term
next_steps: Analyze all identified options and model NPV of each capital scenario
Present a final recommendation to the client with full investment justification to address senior management resistance to new capital spend
